title: Quantum Bicycle LDPC Codes with High $kd^2/n$ from Divisor-Driven Search
authors: Liangdong Lu, Guanmin Guo, Yang Liu, Ruipan Yang
abstract: Bicycle (two-block circulant) quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes include some of the best known small quantum codes, yet their design has relied on group-algebra formulations in which the dimension and distance are accessible only through matrix computation. We show that in the cyclic case the construction collapses into the polynomial ring $\F_2[x]/(x^{l}-1)$: self-orthogonality is automatic, the quantum dimension is read off from a polynomial gcd, and the minimum distance is certified exactly through the Calderbank correspondence to additive codes over $\F_4$, turning code search into an algebraically pre-filtered enumeration that reaches parameter regimes poorly covered by existing tables. A computer search based on this framework recovers the short codes $[[42,12,4]]_2$ and $[[62,12,4]]_2$ and produces a family of codes with competitive figure of merit $kd^2/n$, including $[[66,20,7]]_2$ with $kd^2/n=14.85$, above the bivariate bicycle code $[[144,12,12]]_2$ ($kd^2/n=12$) at less than half the block length, together with $[[46,2,8]]_2$, $[[66,2,9]]_2$, $[[66,4,8]]_2$, $[[66,6,8]]_2$ and, at $n=90$, $[[90,16,6]]_2$, $[[90,18,6]]_2$, $[[90,20,6]]_2$. An exhaustive census at $n=48$ delineates the boundary of this picture: we exhibit a $[[48,10,6]]_2$ code from a minimal $48$-element group (the Aydin--Tamo--Barg realization uses $72$ elements), and prove that distance $5$ forces a stabilizer-rank loss, which excludes $[[48,10,5]]_2$ from the weight-$8$ symmetric coset family. The framework thus opens a systematic route to bicycle-type quantum LDPC codes beyond the reach of group-theoretic searches, and identifies exactly where genuinely coset-theoretic phenomena begin.
summary: This paper develops an advanced algebraic framework to systematically search for high-performing Quantum Bicycle LDPC codes. By translating the complex group-theoretic construction into polynomial ring arithmetic, the authors can efficiently calculate code parameters and discover new optimal codes. This advances the theoretical understanding of quantum error correction capabilities.
main_problem: To systematically design and characterize quantum bicycle Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes by reformulating their construction from group algebra into a purely algebraic/polynomial domain.
main_result: The framework recovers several high-performance codes, such as $[[66, 20, 7]]_2$ with $kd^2/n=14.85$, and establishes structural boundaries by proving the non-existence of certain parameter combinations (e.g., $[[48, 10, 5]]_2$).
method: The authors use a divisor-driven search based on polynomial rings $\mathbb{F}_2[x]/(x^l - 1)$ and relate code properties using the Calderbank correspondence to additive codes over $\mathbb{F}_4$.
model_or_system: The focus is on Quantum Bicycle LDPC codes, which are specific types of CSS quantum error-correcting codes derived from two commuting circulant blocks.
key_observables: Code parameters $[[n, k, d]]_2$, the figure of merit $kd^2/n$, and logical error rates ($p_L$).
important_parameters: The block length $l$ (or $n$), the dimension $k$, and the minimum distance $d$. The search is constrained by polynomial GCDs.
main_assumptions: The initial analysis focuses on the cyclic case, which simplifies the group algebra to a polynomial ring; extending this to general bivariate cases requires more advanced algebraic tools.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate decoding performance plots comparing various codes against reference bounds, and tables list specific code parameters derived from the search framework for different block lengths $n$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the polynomial reformulation of the group-algebraic construction, detailing how to calculate $k$ and $d$ algebraically. It then applies this method via a systematic search to find optimal codes, culminating in structural theorems that define the boundaries of achievable parameters.
why_interesting: This work provides powerful algebraic tools for constructing quantum error-correcting codes, which is fundamental knowledge for anyone working on fault tolerance or quantum computation architectures.
